overview:
In Jain ethics, the "five samitis" (pañca-samiti) are refined disciplines of careful conduct that shape how a practitioner moves, speaks, seeks food, handles objects, and disposes of waste. They are closely linked to the ideal of ahiṃsā (non‑violence) and to the broader framework of gupti (restraint) and samiti (carefulness) that governs the daily life of monks and, in a moderated form, lay followers.

The term samiti derives from the idea of deliberate, mindful regulation of activity. Where gupti emphasizes inner restraint of mind, speech, and body, samiti focuses on the outer expression of that restraint in concrete actions. The five samitis are: (1) iryā‑samiti—carefulness in walking and movement; (2) bhāṣā‑samiti—carefulness in speech; (3) eṣaṇā‑samiti—carefulness in seeking and accepting food and other requisites; (4) ādāna‑nikṣepa‑samiti—carefulness in lifting, placing, and handling objects; and (5) utsarga‑samiti—carefulness in disposing of bodily waste and other materials.

Iryā‑samiti requires that one’s movement be slow, attentive, and non‑injurious, avoiding harm to visible and invisible living beings such as insects or micro‑organisms. This discipline is especially emphasized for ascetics who travel on foot, inspecting the ground and avoiding careless steps. Bhāṣā‑samiti governs speech: speaking truthfully, gently, at the right time, and in a way that does not incite fear, anger, or attachment. It is not only about avoiding lies or harsh words, but also about silence when speech would cause harm.

Eṣaṇā‑samiti regulates the way food and other necessities are sought and received. For monks, this includes rules about where to go for alms, how to avoid causing distress to householders, and how to ensure that the act of taking food does not involve violence, waste, or encouragement of harmful practices. For laypeople, it inspires ethical reflection on livelihood, consumption, and the impact of one’s economic choices on other beings.

Ādāna‑nikṣepa‑samiti concerns the careful handling of objects—picking up, placing down, and using items in ways that minimize harm. This includes checking surfaces before setting things down, avoiding sudden or forceful movements, and being mindful that even small actions (like moving a utensil or opening a door) can affect living beings. Utsarga‑samiti extends this care to the disposal of bodily waste and other materials, ensuring that such acts are done in places and ways that minimize injury and pollution.

Across Jain traditions, the five samitis are treated as foundational disciplines for monastic life and as an ethical ideal for lay practice. They operationalize non‑violence in the smallest details of daily behavior, turning ordinary actions—walking, speaking, eating, handling, discarding—into opportunities for spiritual vigilance. While the strict observance of samitis is most fully realized in ascetic codes, their underlying principles inform broader Jain teachings on environmental care, compassionate communication, and responsible consumption in modern contexts.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation:
Liberation is attained through restraint (gupti), carefulness (samiti), self‑control (saṃyama), austerity (tapas), and the destruction of karma.
The samitis are carefulness in walking (iryā), in speech (bhāṣā), in lifting and placing (ādāna‑nikṣepa), and in disposal (utsarga).
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārtha Sūtra is a key Sanskrit compendium accepted across major Jain traditions. The verses cited summarize the path to liberation and list the samitis in close association with guptis. Some recensions explicitly include eṣaṇā‑samiti (carefulness in seeking alms) in the enumeration, and commentarial traditions clarify that the discipline of alms‑seeking is integral to the full set of five samitis.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārtha Sūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text:
इऱ्यायां प्राणिभ्यः अनवध्यगमनं इऱ्यासमितिः।
सत्यहितमधुरप्रियमितभाषणं भाषासमितिः।
भिक्षाद्येषणायां अनवध्यता एषणासमितिः।
आदान-निक्षेपयोः प्राणिहिंसापरिहारः आादन-निक्षेपसमितिः।
मलोत्सर्गे प्राणिहिंसापरिहारः उत्सर्गसमितिः।
primary_sources.transliteration:
iryāyāṃ prāṇibhyaḥ anavadhya-gamanaṃ iryā-samitiḥ.
satya-hita-madhura-priya-mita-bhāṣaṇaṃ bhāṣā-samitiḥ.
bhikṣādy-eṣaṇāyāṃ anavadhyatā eṣaṇā-samitiḥ.
ādāna-nikṣepayoḥ prāṇi-hiṃsā-parihāraḥ ādāna-nikṣepa-samitiḥ.
malotsarge prāṇi-hiṃsā-parihāraḥ utsarga-samitiḥ.
primary_sources.translation:
In walking, movement that is unobjectionable to living beings is iryā‑samiti.
Speech that is truthful, beneficial, gentle, pleasing, and measured is bhāṣā‑samiti.
In the seeking of alms and similar requisites, being free from blame is eṣaṇā‑samiti.
In lifting and placing, the avoidance of harm to living beings is ādāna‑nikṣepa‑samiti.
In the discharge of waste, the avoidance of harm to living beings is utsarga‑samiti.
primary_sources.notes: Sarvārthasiddhi is a classical Digambara commentary that systematically explains the ethical categories of the Tattvārtha Sūtra. Here, Pūjyapāda explicitly enumerates all five samitis and defines each in terms of non‑violence and blamelessness. The passage clarifies the practical content of the samitis and is widely cited in monastic training and advanced doctrinal study.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Lord Mahāvīra’s teachings; compiled by early Śvetāmbara redactors
primary_sources.translation:
Restraints (gupti), carefulness (samiti), self‑control (saṃyama), and austerities (tapas) are the path to nirvāṇa.
The samitis are: carefulness in walking, carefulness in speech, carefulness in seeking alms, carefulness in lifting and placing, and carefulness in disposal.
primary_sources.notes: The Uttarādhyayana Sūtra is a central Śvetāmbara canonical text in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit. The verses cited reflect the same doctrinal framework as the Tattvārtha Sūtra, but in Prakrit idiom. Different manuscripts vary slightly in wording, yet the fivefold list of samitis is stable across the tradition. This text is frequently used in monastic instruction and lay sermons to introduce the ethical disciplines.

misconceptions.myth: The five samitis are only relevant for monks and have no application to laypeople or modern life.
misconceptions.reality: While the strict, technical observance of samitis is formulated for ascetics, their underlying principles—mindful movement, ethical speech, careful consumption, gentle handling of objects, and responsible disposal—are explicitly extended in Jain teaching to lay practice. Modern interpreters apply these disciplines to issues such as environmental care, non‑violent communication, and ethical livelihood, making them deeply relevant beyond monastic contexts.

misconceptions.myth: Samiti is just another word for general morality and does not have a specific technical meaning.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, samiti is a precise category referring to carefulness in particular bodily and verbal activities. It is distinguished from gupti (inner restraint) and saṃyama (broader self‑control). Treating samiti as a vague synonym for morality obscures its role as a detailed discipline that operationalizes non‑violence in concrete, observable actions.

misconceptions.myth: Eṣaṇā‑samiti only concerns the ritual act of begging for food and has no ethical dimension.
misconceptions.reality: Classical commentaries emphasize that eṣaṇā‑samiti is about blamelessness in seeking and receiving necessities. This includes avoiding distress to donors, ensuring that food is obtained without violence or waste, and reflecting on the karmic implications of one’s dependence on others. For laypeople, the same principle informs ethical choices about livelihood, sourcing of goods, and patterns of consumption.

misconceptions.myth: Ādāna‑nikṣepa‑samiti and utsarga‑samiti are purely ritualistic and concern only minor details of monastic conduct.
misconceptions.reality: Although these samitis are expressed through detailed monastic rules—such as checking the ground before placing objects or choosing appropriate places for waste disposal—their purpose is to prevent harm to even the smallest forms of life and to cultivate continuous awareness. In contemporary application, they support Jain concerns about environmental impact, sanitation, and the subtle ways ordinary actions can contribute to violence or pollution.
